chicken-ns-as-to-part-grilled-without-sa.title: Chicken, grilled without sauce, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is the meat of the domestic bird (Gallus gallus domesticus). In this case it refers to a piece of chicken meat grilled without sauce, with the skin eaten. The dish features the characteristic smoky aroma of the grill, tender meat flavor, and crispy skin.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide.
Grilling preserves most nutrients while adding a distinct smoky flavor.
Chicken skin contains more fat than the meat itself but also provides B‑vitamins and collagen.
When properly grilled, the skin becomes crisp while the meat stays juicy.
Chicken appears in many cuisines, from American barbecue to Asian marinades.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Chicken meat contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It is a good source of niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones, immunity, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Collagen in the skin
items.content: The skin provides collagen, beneficial for skin, joint, and connective‑tissue health.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken or its proteins.

items.title: Fat content in skin
items.content: Chicken skin is high in saturated fat; people monitoring cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken can harbor harmful bacteria such as Salmonella.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: If the meat was marinated in salty solutions before grilling, sodium intake may be elevated.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Grilled chicken breast or thigh can be served as a main dish, sliced into salads, used in sandwiches, or as a taco filling. The skin can be eaten on its own as a crunchy snack or together with the meat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked chicken in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days in an airtight container. For longer storage, freeze for 1‑2 months. Thaw in the fridge, not at room temperature.

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked eggplant is the thermally processed fruit of the eggplant plant (Solanum melongena). After cooking it becomes tender, has a mild flavor and a faint sweetness. It is commonly used in salads, stews, casseroles and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggplant belongs to the nightshade family and is a relative of tomatoes, potatoes and peppers.
It contains anthocyanins that give the characteristic purple color and act as antioxidants.
Different cuisines treat eggplant differently: Mediterranean cuisine often grills it, Asian cuisine stews it, and in Russian tradition it is frequently boiled or baked.
Eggplant can absorb up to 90 % of its weight in water, so it retains a lot of moisture during cooking.
There are more than 300 varieties of eggplant, varying in shape, size and skin hue.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and vitamin C help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Potassium content and low saturated fat support normal blood pressure.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B6 and folate are involved in protein metabolism and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: One cup of cooked eggplant provides about 35 kcal, making it a good choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to eggplant.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Eggplant contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Nutrient loss with prolonged cooking
items.content: Overcooking can reduce vitamin C and some polyphenols.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked eggplant can be diced for salads, added to vegetable stews, baked with cheese, or served as a side to meat and fish. It also works well pureed for dips and sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked eggplant in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer keeping, freeze in portions in freezer‑safe bags, where it retains quality for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned tuna is fish from the mackerel family, caught in open oceans, heat‑processed and sealed in airtight cans with its own juice, oil, or tomato sauce. The canning process preserves most nutrients, gives a tender texture, and a characteristic sea flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna is one of the fastest marine predators, capable of swimming up to 75 km/h.
Most canned tuna comes from skipjack and yellowfin species.
Canning allows the fish to be stored for several years without added preservatives.
Tuna is used in traditional dishes worldwide: sushi in Japan, salads in the Mediterranean, and sandwiches in the United States.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Tuna provides EPA and DHA, which support heart health, vascular function, and normal brain activity.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A typical serving (≈100 g) delivers about 25 g of complete animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna is a good source of B12, B6, and niacin, which aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals: selenium and iodine
items.content: Selenium protects cells from oxidative stress, while iodine is vital for proper thyroid function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many meat products, tuna contains relatively little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: Tuna can accumulate mercury; pregnant or nursing women and young children should limit intake.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including tuna.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Canned tuna often contains added salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you monitor sodium intake.

items.title: Bacterial growth after opening
items.content: Once opened, store tuna in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 2‑3 days to prevent bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned tuna can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, pasta, sandwiches, sushi rolls, or used as a filling for pies. It pairs well with olive oil, lemon, herbs, and fresh vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct light. After opening, transfer the tuna to an airtight container and refrigerate, using it within 2‑3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit butter is a thick, aromatic spread made by slowly cooking ripe fruits with a small amount of sugar and sometimes spices. The result is a smooth paste with a pronounced fruit flavor, perfect for spreading on bread, using in baking, or as a filling for desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fruit butter has a long tradition in Eastern European countries, especially Poland and Russia.
Common fruits used include apples, pears, apricots, cherries and plums.
Unlike jam, fruit butter has a completely smooth texture without fruit pieces.
The high sugar content gives fruit butter a longer shelf life than fresh fruit.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Fruit butter provides B‑vitamins, vitamin C and carotenoids, which support immunity and vision.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids normal digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Natural antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds in fruit butter protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Naturally occurring fruit sugars deliver a quick source of energy.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The large amount of sugar may be unsuitable for people with diabetes or those monitoring blood glucose.

items.title: Fruit allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to specific fruits used in the butter.

items.title: Additive presence
items.content: Commercial versions may contain preservatives or additives; choose products without artificial ingredients when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fruit butter can be spread on bread, pancakes, toast, used as a filling for pies, cupcakes and cheese cakes, or stirred into yogurt, cottage cheese or smoothies to boost flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fruit butter in a tightly sealed jar in the refrigerator. When kept properly, it retains its taste and quality for up to 3 months. Discard if mold appears or the aroma changes.

macaroni-or-noodles-with-cheese-and-meat.title: Macaroni or noodles with cheese and meat (Hamburger Helper mix 3580)

content.title: About
content.content: A ready‑to‑cook kit of macaroni (or noodles) with a cheesy sauce and meat pieces, prepared using the Hamburger Helper mix (item 3580). It is a hearty, quick‑preparation meal suitable for family lunches.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hamburger Helper was first introduced in the United States in 1971 as a fast way to make a meat‑and‑macaroni dish.
The mix contains only dry ingredients; fresh water, milk and meat are added during cooking.
The dish is popular with children because of its soft pasta texture and mild cheese flavor.
The original recipe calls for ground beef, but chicken, turkey or plant‑based crumbles can be used instead.
The dry mix stores well for up to two years when kept in a cool, dry place.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Meat and the dry mix provide a substantial amount of protein needed for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The cheese sauce supplies calcium for bone health, while vitamin D aids its absorption.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from the pasta give a quick source of energy, useful during active days.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The fortified mix contains B1, B2 and niacin, which support metabolic processes.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Meat contributes iron, essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The dry mix can be high in salt; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Contains dairy, gluten and soy, which are common allergens.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑rich due to cheese and meat, so consider overall daily energy balance.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese adds saturated fat, which may affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bring a pot of water to a boil, add the macaroni and cook 5–7 minutes. Drain, return pasta to the pot, stir in milk and the dry mix. Add pre‑cooked meat, simmer another 2–3 minutes until the sauce thickens.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry mix in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from moisture and direct sunlight. Once opened, use within six months.

content.title: About
content.content: Dried prunes are the dehydrated fruits of the plum tree (Prunus domestica), traditionally cultivated in temperate regions of Europe and Asia. Drying removes most of the water while preserving the sweet flavor, chewy texture, and concentrated nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dried prunes are naturally high in sugars, making them a popular natural sweetener in cooking.
Plums belong to the same family as cherries, apricots, and almonds.
In ancient Rome, dried prunes were used as a remedy for constipation.
When stored properly, dried prunes can keep for up to a year.
Plums are a source of antioxidants, especially polyphenols.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, helps regulate bowel movements, and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Polysaccharides and phenolic compounds protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Boron and magnesium content contribute to stronger bones.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Dried prunes have a high glycemic index, so people with diabetes should limit their intake.

items.title: Plum allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to plums.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Large portions can cause gas and discomfort due to the high sugar and fiber levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried prunes can be enjoyed as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, baked goods, salads, or used in sauces and compotes. They are often soaked in water to rehydrate before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried prunes in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent mold growth.
